description.en: Two-party negotiation companion for HIPAA Business Associate Agreements under 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, built on an attested springing, no-PHI-by-design base template. Instrument screen (run before negotiating any option): a BAA is required only when the vendor creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of a covered entity or business associate; if the vendor never touches PHI in any form, a BAA is not required, and signing one anyway is not free protection; if the services DO involve PHI, by design or in routine fact, this springing template is the wrong instrument and the deal needs a conventional BAA. Housing (choose before the options): HHS expressly blesses both routes, a standalone BAA or provisions incorporated into an agreement for the provision of services; this pack is the standalone instrument, which references and leans on the Underlying Agreement. GDPR note: a HIPAA-compliant BAA does not satisfy Art. 28 GDPR, and a GDPR-compliant DPA does not satisfy 45 CFR 164.504(e); where personal data of EU/EEA data subjects can reach the vendor, the deal needs the BAA plus a GDPR rider or a standalone DPA, and a springing DPA is not a recognised GDPR instrument. Governing law carries a California default and venue is a party-designated bracket the parties complete in Section 21(c); confirm before use. Software work-product tooling, not legal advice; requires supervised use by a licensed professional.

title.en: Section 8. Report of Security Incidents (satisfies 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(C) in part; satisfies 45 CFR 164.314(a)(2)(i)(C))

plainDescription.en: Sets the clock for reporting successful Security Incidents, and gives blanket, once-for-all notice of attempted but unsuccessful incidents (pings, port scans, failed log-ins, denials of service) so neither party drowns in noise. The blanket notice is valid only while no incident results in unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of PHI.

legalContext.en: The Security Rule's organizational terms require the contract to provide for security-incident reporting (45 CFR 164.314(a)(2)(i)(C)), but the regulation does not fix a numeric clock for these reports: the contract sets it. Every option here, including 72 hours, is market practice, not law. The blanket-notice device for unsuccessful attempts is defensible only while limited to incidents with no unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of PHI. This Section's narrow definition of discovery applies to Section 8 only; Section 9 (Report of Breach) stays governed by the definition at 45 CFR 164.410(a)(2). HHS sample position: the official sample requires the vendor to report any security incident it becomes aware of, but sets no deadline and has no noise filter for failed attacks, so both the clock and the blanket-notice device are pure negotiation.

plainDescription.en: Favors: the vendor. It gets more than a week to investigate before it must say anything, while the customer waits unaware.

en: Room to investigate before reporting
Fewer false alarms escalated
A customer with regulated downstream duties may see this as slow
Reports that arrive are triaged and meaningful
Up to roughly 9 to 11 calendar days of not knowing about a successful incident on systems adjacent to its data

legalText.en:
The parties acknowledge and agree that this Section constitutes notice by Company to Customer of the ongoing existence of attempted but unsuccessful Security Incidents on Company's networks, including pings and other broadcast attacks on Company's firewall, port scans, unsuccessful log-on attempts, denials of service, and any combination of the foregoing, so long as no such incident results in unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of PHI, and no additional notice of such attempted-but-unsuccessful incidents shall be required.

Company shall report to Customer, without unreasonable delay and in no event later than seven (7) business days after discovery, any successful Security Incident of which Company becomes aware. For purposes of this Section 8 only, "discovery" means the first day on which the incident is actually known to Company's designated Security Official or to any member of Company's security or incident-response team acting in that capacity. The definition of "discovery" in this Section 8 does not apply to Section 9 (Report of Breach), which is governed by the definition at 45 CFR 164.410(a)(2).

plainDescription.en: Favors: neither party strongly; the vendor still gets time to establish the facts and the customer hears meaningfully sooner.

en: Balanced investigation window

title.en: Section 9. Report of Breach (satisfies 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(C); tracks 45 CFR 164.410)

plainDescription.en: Sets how fast the vendor must report a Breach of Unsecured PHI to the customer after discovery, as defined at 45 CFR 164.410(a)(2). The report must always also be without unreasonable delay; the day count is an outer limit, not an entitlement to wait.

legalContext.en: Regulatory floor: 45 CFR 164.410(b) requires the report without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days from discovery. No contract can extend this, which is why no option at or beyond that outer bound exists in this pack. The definition of discovery is fixed text pinned to 45 CFR 164.410(a)(2), including imputation of knowledge under a reasonable-diligence standard; it is not negotiable currency. Imputation trap: if the vendor acts as the customer's agent under the federal common law of agency, the customer is treated as discovering the breach when the vendor discovers it (45 CFR 164.404(a)(2)), so every day of vendor reporting time is a day burned off the customer's own 60-calendar-day individual-notification clock (45 CFR 164.404(b)); in an agency posture the customer fairly insists on a much shorter clock, and which side of the agency line the deal sits on is a call for the supervising lawyer. HHS sample position: the official sample requires breach reporting only as required at 45 CFR 164.410 with no number of its own, and its bracketed note expressly invites the parties to agree a stricter timeframe and to decide who handles the notifications to individuals, regulators, and the media.

plainDescription.en: Favors: neither party strongly; about a week for the vendor to get the facts straight, with most of the deadline preserved for the customer.

en: Balanced investigation window
Aligns with the Section 3 inadvertent-receipt notice window
Strong position; leaves most of the customer's own window intact

legalText.en:
Company shall report to Customer any use or disclosure of PHI not permitted by this Agreement, including any Breach of Unsecured PHI as required by 45 CFR 164.410. Company will make such report without unreasonable delay and in no event later than five (5) business days after discovery of the Breach. For purposes of this Section, "discovery" has the meaning given at 45 CFR 164.410(a)(2), including the imputation of knowledge to any workforce member or agent of Company (other than the individual committing the Breach) under a reasonable-diligence standard.

Company's report shall include, to the extent then known and thereafter as further information becomes available: (a) the identification of each individual whose Unsecured PHI has been, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed; (b) a description of what happened, including the date of the Breach and the date of discovery; (c) a description of the types of Unsecured PHI involved; (d) the steps Company has taken or will take to investigate, mitigate harm to individuals, and protect against further Breaches; and (e) such other information as Customer may reasonably request to complete a risk assessment under 45 CFR 164.402 or to make notifications under 45 CFR 164.404, 45 CFR 164.406, and 45 CFR 164.408.

As between the parties, Customer is responsible for performing the risk assessment described in 45 CFR 164.402 and for all notifications to individuals, the media, and the Secretary under 45 CFR 164.404, 45 CFR 164.406, and 45 CFR 164.408. Company shall reasonably cooperate with Customer's risk assessment and notification process, including by providing supplemental factual information within its knowledge on reasonable request.

If, and only if, the PHI concerned was transmitted to Company in violation of Section 2 and the Breach was not caused by Company's failure to comply with the Security Rule or this Agreement, Customer shall bear the reasonable costs of Breach investigation, notification, and remediation. Customer shall use reasonable efforts to inform Company of any compromise of its own systems that may affect Company.

title.en: Section 10. Individual Access to PHI (satisfies 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(E))

plainDescription.en: When the vendor holds PHI in a Designated Record Set, it must hand that PHI to the customer, or to the individual at the customer's direction, fast enough for the customer to honor an individual's access request under 45 CFR 164.524. Direct requests from individuals are routed to the customer, not answered by the vendor.

legalContext.en: 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(E) requires the BAA to make PHI available for individual access per 45 CFR 164.524; the provision itself is required, and the internal turnaround number is contractual. Context floor: the covered entity itself must act on an access request within 30 days (45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i)), with one extension of no more than 30 days; the combined vendor and customer time must fit inside that window or the clause sets the customer up to violate 45 CFR 164.524. HHS sample position: the official sample imposes the access duty but leaves the recipient as a bracketed choice and, in its own words, leaves the timeframe for the business associate to provide the information to the covered entity and the handling of direct individual requests for the parties to fill in.

plainDescription.en: Favors: neither party strongly; workable for a vendor with electronic records, and the customer keeps half its deadline for its own steps.

en: Still workable where records are electronic
Hard if data is sharded across systems
Half the window preserved for its own processing and delivery

legalText.en: To the extent Company maintains PHI in a Designated Record Set on behalf of Customer, Company shall make such PHI available to Customer, or, at Customer's written direction, to the individual to whom it pertains or the individual's designee, as necessary to enable Customer to satisfy its obligations under 45 CFR 164.524. Company shall make such PHI available within fifteen (15) calendar days of Customer's written request, in the form and format reasonably requested to the extent readily producible in that form and format, and otherwise in a readable electronic form and format as agreed by the parties. If Company receives a request for access directly from an individual, Company shall promptly forward the request to Customer and shall not respond substantively except at Customer's direction.

title.en: Section 15. Term and Termination (satisfies the termination-for-cause authorization at 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(iii); §15(d) consistent with 45 CFR 164.504(e)(1)(iii))

plainDescription.en: If the vendor materially violates the BAA, the customer may terminate the BAA and the underlying services agreement unless the vendor cures within the window; if cure is not feasible, termination is immediate. Only the customer-side cure window in Section 15(b) varies across the options; the rest of the Section is fixed.

legalContext.en: Termination-for-cause capability is a required element (45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(iii)); no option may delete it. The cure number is contractual. The sentence allowing immediate termination when cure is not feasible stays under every option, and the thirty-day Company-side cure window in Section 15(c) is fixed text, not part of this option set. Drafting integrity: whatever option is chosen, words and numerals must agree; a prior draft's word and numeral disagreement, forty-five (15), is a classic latent-ambiguity exploit at the termination moment. HHS sample position: the official sample makes the cure opportunity itself optional bracketed language, and even where included the cure time is whatever is specified by covered entity, a customer-leaning default with no number attached.

plainDescription.en: Favors: neither party strongly; enough time to fix real problems, with immediate exit still available for the unfixable ones.

en: Standard; enough for most cures
Standard; the immediate-if-incurable sentence covers the emergencies

legalText.en:
(a) Term. This Agreement is effective on the date last signed below and continues in effect until terminated in accordance with this Section 15 or until all PHI received by Company from, or created, received, maintained, or transmitted on behalf of, Customer has been returned or destroyed in accordance with Section 16, whichever is later.

(b) Termination for Cause by Customer. Customer may terminate this Agreement and the Underlying Agreement if Customer determines that Company has violated a material term of this Agreement and Company has not cured the violation, or is not capable of curing the violation, within thirty (30) calendar days after written notice from Customer describing the violation in reasonable detail. If cure is not feasible, Customer may terminate immediately on written notice.

(c) Termination for Cause by Company. Company may terminate this Agreement and, at its election, the Underlying Agreement on written notice if Customer has violated a material term of this Agreement and has not cured the violation within thirty (30) calendar days after written notice from Company describing the violation in reasonable detail. A material breach by Customer includes, without limitation, a knowing or repeated transmission of PHI to Company in violation of Section 2.

(d) Knowledge of Pattern of Activity by Subcontractors. If Company knows of a pattern of activity or practice of a Subcontractor that constitutes a material breach or violation of the Subcontractor's obligation under its written agreement with Company that mirrors this Agreement, Company shall take reasonable steps to cure the breach or end the violation, and, if such steps are unsuccessful, terminate the arrangement with the Subcontractor, if feasible, consistent with 45 CFR 164.504(e)(1)(iii).

plainDescription.en: Favors: the vendor. A vendor accused of a serious violation keeps operating for six-plus weeks while it tries to fix things.

en: Real remediation time for systemic fixes

title.en: Section 16. Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination (satisfies 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J))

plainDescription.en: At termination, the vendor returns or destroys all PHI it still holds, within the disposition window; if return or destruction is infeasible, protections extend to the retained PHI for as long as it is held. Only the disposition window in Section 16(a) varies across the options; the infeasibility-notice thirty days in Section 16(b) is fixed text.

legalContext.en: 45 CFR 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J) makes return or destruction at termination if feasible, with extension of protections if not, a required provision; no option deletes it. Destruction must render PHI unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable per the guidance issued under section 13402(h)(2) of Public Law 111-5, cross-referenced in the Unsecured-PHI definition at 45 CFR 164.402. HHS guidance carried in the template: business convenience alone does not make return or destruction infeasible. The infeasibility gate is mutual agreement, not the vendor's own determination. HHS sample position: the official sample requires return of all health data at termination with no time period stated, allows destruction only if agreed to by covered entity, offers a bracketed retention alternative limited to the vendor's own management, administration, or legal responsibilities, and never mentions infeasibility.

plainDescription.en: Favors: the healthcare customer. Fast, clean closure after the relationship ends; the vendor may need a carve-out for backups.

en: Achievable for primary stores
May need a backup-cycle carve-out
Clean, fast closure

legalText.en:
(a) Return or Destruction. On termination of this Agreement, for any reason, Company shall, if feasible, return to Customer or destroy all PHI received from, or created, received, maintained, or transmitted on behalf of, Customer that Company still maintains in any form, and shall retain no copies of such PHI. Company shall complete such return or destruction within thirty (30) calendar days of the effective date of termination, or such longer period as the parties agree in writing. Destruction shall be carried out in a manner consistent with applicable guidance issued by the Secretary under section 13402(h)(2) of Public Law 111-5 (cross-referenced in the definition of Unsecured Protected Health Information at 45 CFR 164.402), under which PHI is rendered unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable to unauthorized persons.

(b) Infeasibility. If Company determines that return or destruction of PHI is not feasible, Company shall provide Customer, within thirty (30) calendar days of termination, with written notification of the conditions that make return or destruction infeasible. On mutual agreement of the parties that return or destruction of PHI is infeasible, Company shall extend the protections of this Agreement to such PHI and limit further uses and disclosures of such PHI to those purposes that make the return or destruction infeasible, for so long as Company maintains such PHI. The parties acknowledge and agree that, consistent with guidance issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, retention of PHI merely for Company's own business convenience does not, without more, render return or destruction infeasible.

(c) Subcontractors. Company shall require each Subcontractor that received PHI under this Agreement to return, destroy, or continue to protect such PHI on the same terms set forth in this Section 16.

(d) Springing Structure. Deletion or return pursuant to Section 3 satisfies this Section 16 as to the PHI concerned.

plainDescription.en: Favors: neither party strongly; a workable compromise for ordinary systems.

en: Comfortable
Acceptable

The parties acknowledge and agree that, consistent with guidance issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, retention of PHI merely for Company's own business convenience does not, without more, render return or destruction infeasible.

(c) Subcontractors. Company shall require each Subcontractor that received PHI under this Agreement to return, destroy, or continue to protect such PHI on the same terms set forth in this Section 16.

(d) Springing Structure. Deletion or return pursuant to Section 3 satisfies this Section 16 as to the PHI concerned.

plainDescription.en: By default, claims under the BAA live inside the services agreement's indemnities and liability cap. The negotiation is whether HIPAA-flavored liability (the vendor's Security Rule failures, impermissible use or disclosure under Section 5, vendor-caused Breaches of Unsecured PHI) stays inside the ordinary cap, gets a raised supercap, or runs uncapped for the worst conduct. Only the final sentence of Section 19(b) varies across the options; the Section 19(a) customer indemnity for Section 2 violations is fixed.

legalContext.en: Direct liability, in plain words: the vendor is directly answerable to the government under the HIPAA Rules, with civil and in some cases criminal penalties, no matter what this contract says; so is the customer for its own duties. No cap in this clause touches that answerability; the options only decide how the two companies split what is left between them. As between the parties, allocation is free, but a cap clause that reads as limiting an individual's or regulator's recourse is a defect, not an option. Current enforcement-framework figures are not verified in this pack; confirm against primary sources before quoting numbers. HHS sample position: the official sample contains no liability, indemnity, insurance, or cap provisions of any kind; the entire money conversation is pure negotiation.
